The '''Gathang language''', also spelt '''Gadjang''', '''Katang''', '''Kattang''', '''Kutthung''', '''Gadhang''', '''Gadang''' and previously known as '''Worimi''' (also spelt Warrimay), is an [[Australian Aboriginal language]] or group of dialects. The three known dialects are '''Birrbay''', '''Guringay''', and '''Warrimay''', which are used by the [[Worimi people|Worimi]], [[Guringay]], and [[Birrbay]] peoples. It went [[extinct language|extinct]] during the latter half of the 20th century, but has been [[language revival|revived]] in the 21st century.

==History and status==
After the [[colonisation of Australia]], many of the hundreds of Aboriginal languages fell into disuse. The Worimi people comprised 18 clan groups (''ngurras''), all of whom spoke Gathang. The four ngurras of the [[Port Stephens, New South Wales|Port Stephens]] area moved to the settlement at [[Carrington, New South Wales|Carrington]] to work at the [[Australian Agricultural Company]], and over the years lost their language and culture as they learnt European ways. Many Worimi people were forced into missions and [[Aboriginal reserve|reserve]]s.<ref name=wcl>{{cite web | title=The Worimi | website=Worimi Conservation Lands | date=23 December 2020 | url=https://worimiconservationlands.com/the-worimi-warrimay-have-always-been-and-remain-today-the-traditional-custodians-of-a-large-area-of-land-the-worimi-nation-oral-history-passed-down-by-the-elders-record-that-the-w/ | access-date=9 August 2023}}</ref>

In 1887: [[E.M. Curr]] published the first word list of the Gathang language, which had been compiled by John Branch, and in 1900, [[Walter John Enright|W.J. Enright]] published a description and word list. In 1929, American linguist [[Gerhardt Laves]] worked with Gathang speakers Charlie Briggs, Bill Dungie, Charlie Bugg, Jim Moy, Albert Lobban, Hannah Bugg, Susan Russell, Ted Lobban, and Mrs Russell.<ref name=muurrbay/> During the 1960s, Swedish linguist [[Nils Holmer]] made recordings of two Worimi [[Aboriginal elder|elders]], Eddie Lobban and Fred Bugg, and compiled a [[grammar]] of the Gathang language.<ref name=wcl/><ref>{{cite book|last=Holmer|first=Nils M.|author-link=Nils Holmer|title=An Attempt towards a Comparative Grammar of Two Australian Languages|year=1966|publisher=[[Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies]]|location=Canberra}}</ref><ref name=muurrbay/>

For many years the language appeared to be [[language extinction|extinct]], but [[language revitalisation|revitalisation]] has been under way in the 21st century. In 2010, ''A Grammar and Dictionary of Gathang: The Language of the Birrbay, Guringay and Warrimay'', by Amanda Lissarrague, was published,<ref name=lissarague2010>{{cite book | last=Lissarrague | first=Amanda | title=A Grammar and Dictionary of Gathang: The Language of the Birrbay, Guringay and Warrimay | publisher=Muurrbay Aboriginal Language & Culture Co-operative | year=2010 | isbn=978-0-9775351-7-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6b68cQAACAAJ | access-date=11 August 2023 | page=}}</ref> and the [[Muurrbay Aboriginal Language and Culture Co-operative]] started running classes in [[Taree]], [[Forster, New South Wales|Forster]], and [[Port Macquarie]]. The number of speakers soon grew, and classes were introduced at [[TAFE NSW|TAFEs]], schools, and within family groups.<ref name=muurrbay>{{cite web | title=Gathang (Birrbay, Guringay & Warrimay) | website=Muurrbay Aboriginal Language and Culture Co-operative | url=https://muurrbay.org.au/languages/gathang/ | access-date=11 August 2023}}</ref> As of 2014, there were 40 recorded speakers of the language, and by 2018-2019 there were more than a thousand,<ref name=aiatsis>{{AIATSIS|E67}}</ref> after work had been done on reviving the language.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2019-04-03/revitalising-the-aboriginal-language-gathang/10959142|title=Revitalising the Aboriginal language Gathang is about learning and speaking it together every day|last=Sati|first=Wiriya|date=2 April 2019|work=ABC news|access-date=12 September 2019}}</ref> Today, books, songs, dance, [[storytelling]], and language workshops are all used to help revive and preserve the language,<ref name=wcl/> and it is being studied at [[PhD]] level.<ref name=muurrbay/>

==Classification==
Gathang is closely related to [[Awabakal language|Awabakal]], in the [[Yuin–Kuric languages|Yuin–Kuric group]] of [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan]].<ref name=aiatsis/> Gathang is the language name covering three dialects: Birrbay, Guringay, and Warrimay.<ref name=muurrbay/>

Within the [[orthography]], both [[Voice (phonetics)|voiceless and voiced]] [[Stop (phonetics)|stops]] are written, words begin with voiced stops only and only voiced stops may occur in consonant clusters or suffixes. There is some inconsistency in the orthography to choice of stop intervocalically. The dictionary/grammar written by Lissarrague prescribes voiceless stops intervocalically, but this is violated many times such as in ''magu'' - axe. The phonemes /p/ and /b/ may contrast, such as ''gaparr'' - baby, boy, and ''gabarr'' - head. This is unclear.<ref name=lissarague2010/>

There is some evidence of a merger of the dental and palatal stops/[[Nasal consonant|nasals]], with free variation existing in many words, such as ''djinggarr~dhinggarr'' - silver, grey.<ref name=lissarague2010/>

At the end of a word, a nasal may also be pronounced as its corresponding stop. (E.g. ''bakan~bakat'' - rock).<ref name=lissarague2010/>

Intervocalically, "b" may be pronounced as [v].<ref name=lissarague2010/>

==Vocabulary==
Some Gathang words are:<ref name=wcl/>
*{{lang|kda|Barrgan}} ([[boomerang]]s)
*{{lang|kda|Wamarr}} ([[Woomera (spear-thrower)|woomeras]]
*{{lang|kda|Ganay}} ([[digging stick]]s)
*{{lang|kda|Garrigay}} (wild [[List of plants known as myrtle#Non-Australian natives, not in Myrtaceae|myrtle]]) 
*{{lang|kda|Buwatja}} (food)
*{{lang|kda|Ngapuwi}} (freshwater)
*{{lang|kda|Duumala}} ([[stream|creeks]])
*{{lang|kda|Bami}} (rivers)
*{{lang|kda|Ganya}} ([[humpy|bark huts]])
*{{lang|kda|Wirray}} (bush)

There are many place names in New South Wales which have names ascribed to them in the Gathang language, including:<ref name=wcl/>
* ''Birubi'' ("[[Southern Cross]]" or "view of the Southern Cross")
* ''Tanilba'' ("place of white flowers")
* ''Mallabula'' ("swampland between two mountains")
* ''Karuah'' ("place of [[native plum]] tree")
* ''Pindimar'' ("place of black [[Phalangeriformes|possum]]s")
